note: Home side of The Charge Sheet: home chargers, home batteries and EVs (with bidirectional capability). Prices are US list or typical installed figures as of September 2026, rounded. Battery prices are installed; charger prices are hardware only. Vehicle battery sizes are approximate usable capacity. Check the source before relying on any single number.

chargers.blurb: Hardwired 48 amp wall box with a Tesla plug and a J1772 adapter that swings out. Charges nearly anything sold in the US. Paired with a Powerwall 3, it also lets a new Model 3 or Model Y back up the house.

chargers.blurb: The cheap way around a full panel. It watches the whole house and turns itself down when the dryer and the oven are running.
A metal box with no app and no opinions. Schedule charging from the car instead.
The same tank of a box, hardwired at 48 amps, with an app bolted on.

chargers.loadMgmt: Gateway isolates the home from the grid

chargers.loadMgmt: Power Recovery Unit handles the switch to backup
chargers.source: Kia and Wallbox, 2026. $6,440 before install; Kia EV9 only so far, in select states
chargers.blurb: A DC bidirectional charger, so the power conversion happens in the box instead of the car. Kia EV9 for now.

chargers.source: dcbel and pv magazine, 2026. Price and power approximate; California program first
chargers.blurb: A DC bidirectional charger with a solar inverter inside. Supports the Volvo EX90, Polestar 3 and Nissan Leaf so far, mostly in California.

Long-life cells and a small inverter. An essentials battery unless you stack it.

gasNote: EPA combined MPG for a common trim, via Edmunds' model-year MPG pages (fueleconomy.gov ratings), September 2026. Premium means the maker requires or recommends it. Tank is the standard fuel tank for that trim in gallons, from maker and Kelley Blue Book spec pages, October 2026; trucks and AWD versions vary by cab and drivetrain.

panel.priceNote: Hardware, $825 to $955 from distributors. Installed cost not published.
panel.how: Sensors on the main feed watch the whole house and cut power to the charger when the house passes 80% of the main breaker, then turn it back on after 15 minutes below that.
panel.installNote: Electrician installs it between the meter and the main panel and lands the charger on it.
panel.listing: CSA and UL listed (standard not named by the maker)
panel.worksWith: Any hardwired charger. It switches power to the charger rather than talking to it.
panel.blurb: A gray box that switches the charger off when the house gets close to its limit. Not clever, but it works with any charger and has done this job in Quebec for years.

panel.priceNote: Suggested price for the controller. Installation extra.
panel.how: Clamps on the main service watch total load and pause the charger circuit when the house goes over 80% of panel capacity.
panel.listing: UL Listed, file E510161 (standard not named on the product page)
panel.worksWith: Any charger. It switches the circuit.
panel.blurb: The cheapest whole-house watchdog here. It does not slow the car down, it just turns it off until the oven is done.

panel.priceNote: Tesla shop price. Often out of stock, and Tesla asks for proof you own a Tesla product.
panel.how: Two 200 A sensors on the mains report live house load, and the Wall Connector raises or lowers its charge rate to stay under the limit the installer set.
panel.listing: Not published. Tesla approves it as a load management device with Gen 3 and Universal Wall Connectors.
panel.worksWith: Tesla Gen 3 Wall Connector and Universal Wall Connector only.
panel.app: Yes, through the Tesla app and installer setup.
panel.blurb: If you already own a Wall Connector, this is the cheapest way to make it panel-aware. When it is in stock.

panel.how: The meter measures house load in real time and the Pulsar Plus lowers or raises its charge rate to keep the panel under its limit.
panel.installNote: Electrician fits the DIN-rail meter and two clamps in the panel.
panel.app: Yes, Power Boost is switched on in the myWallbox app.
panel.blurb: Teaches a Pulsar Plus to back off when the air conditioner kicks on. Only works with Wallbox chargers.

panel.kind: Charger with load management built in
panel.priceNote: Hardwired version, third-party price; the plug-in one is about $999. Needs an Enphase IQ Gateway.
panel.how: Sensors on the service tell the Enphase Gateway what the house is drawing, and it slows the charger so the house stays under a limit of up to 80% of the main breaker.
panel.installNote: Qualified electrician, plus consumption sensors and an IQ Gateway.
panel.worksWith: Itself. Needs the Enphase IQ Gateway.
panel.blurb: Makes sense if you already have Enphase solar and a Gateway. Without one, you are buying a small ecosystem to charge a car.

panel.kind: Charger with load management built in
panel.priceNote: List price at launch, August 2026. Hardwired only for now.
panel.how: Current sensors in the box watch the house over a wire, and the charger slows down or speeds up to stay within the service.
panel.listing: UL 3141 certified system, accepted for load calculations where the inspector allows it
panel.blurb: A charger with the sensors in the box and the UL 3141 listing inspectors increasingly ask for.

panel.how: The dryer and the car plug into the splitter. When the dryer starts the car pauses, and when it stops the car carries on.
panel.installNote: Plugs into the existing dryer outlet. The maker says no electrician or permit.
panel.listing: cUL Listed (standard not named by the maker)
panel.worksWith: Any charger set to 24 A or less.
panel.blurb: Shares the dryer outlet with the car and pauses the car when the dryer runs. Some utilities have rebated it.

panel.how: Splits one 50 A outlet into two and keeps the combined draw at 40 A, 20 A each when both sides are charging.
panel.installNote: Plugs into an existing 50 A outlet.
panel.listing: cUL Listed (standard not named by the maker)
panel.worksWith: Any charger. The total is capped at 40 A.
panel.blurb: Mostly sold for two cars on one 14-50. How it behaves with a range on the other side is not something the maker spells out.

panel.priceNote: Maker price. Refurbished units sell for less.
panel.how: Senses when the dryer runs, gives it full power until the cycle ends, then switches back to the car.
panel.installNote: Plugs into a 30 A dryer outlet. Set the charger to 24 A by hand.
panel.blurb: Same idea as NeoCharge, a few dollars cheaper and no app.

panel.how: Wired between one breaker and two loads. When the priority load (range, dryer, heat pump) runs, the charger is cut off, and it comes back five minutes after the priority load stops.
panel.installNote: Licensed electrician, hardwired, about half an hour of work.
panel.listing: UL 916 (energy management equipment), CSA C22.2 No. 205
panel.worksWith: Any charger set to 48 A or less.
panel.blurb: The permanent, inspector-friendly version of a splitter: a box on the wall instead of a plug behind the dryer.

panel.priceNote: Maker price. An automatic version is also sold.
panel.how: A manual switch sends the dryer outlet to either the dryer or the car, never both.
panel.worksWith: Any charger kept at 24 A or less.
panel.blurb: The original version: you flip a switch. Works until someone forgets and the laundry sits there damp.

panel.priceNote: Hardware. The range runs from $2,550 (MLO 24) to $4,100 (MAIN 40). Installation is a panel swap, so get itemized quotes.
panel.how: Every circuit runs through a relay, and the panel throttles or sheds chosen loads, mainly the charger, to keep the service under its limit.
panel.installNote: SPAN-authorized electrician replaces the main panel, 3 to 8 hours.
panel.worksWith: Any charger on a managed circuit. SPAN also sells its own 48 A charger, only with the panel.
panel.blurb: The full replacement: a new panel where every breaker answers to your phone. Often costs more than the upgrade you were avoiding, but you get something for it.

panel.priceNote: No published price. Third-party estimates run $4,000 to $6,700 installed, unverified.
panel.how: Sits beside your panel, watches total load, and switches off chosen circuits so the house stays under its service limit.
panel.installNote: Electrician mounts it next to the panel and moves selected circuits through it.
panel.worksWith: Any charger on a managed circuit.
panel.blurb: Smart-panel control without ripping out the panel you have.

panel.model: Smart breakers + Whole Home Energy Monitor
panel.priceNote: The monitor is $391. Two-pole smart breakers run about $75 to $200 each.
panel.how: Smart breakers can be switched off remotely or on a schedule, and the monitor tracks whole-home use.
panel.installNote: Electrician swaps breakers in an existing Leviton panel and adds the monitor.
panel.listing: Not published on the store pages.
panel.worksWith: Any charger on a smart breaker, manual or scheduled control.
panel.blurb: The cheapest way into a smart panel if you already have a Leviton one. Leviton does not sell it as automatic EV load management, so it will not help you skip an upgrade.

panel.priceNote: No current price. 2022 maker pricing was modules from $60 a circuit and the Director from $500.
panel.how: Smart modules replace breakers in a standard panel, and a power budget sheds loads in real time to stay within the service.
panel.worksWith: Any charger on a managed circuit.
panel.blurb: The smart-home company’s take on the smart panel. Good if you are already a Savant house, a lot of dealer otherwise.

rtc.hoa: Condos, HOAs, co-ops and community apartments
rtc.renters: Yes, landlord must approve a written request on qualifying properties
points: The association cannot ban a charger in your own space, only add reasonable rules that don’t significantly raise the cost.
You pay for installation, electricity and upkeep, use a licensed contractor, and carry a $1 million umbrella policy naming the association.
Renters: the landlord must say yes to a written request on most properties; you pay, and carry liability insurance unless the charger is certified and an electrician does the work.

rtc.renters: Yes, a tenant may install a charger at their own expense
points: An association cannot prohibit a Level 1 or Level 2 charger in your space, or charge you a fee for it beyond the electricity.
You hire a licensed electrician, follow reasonable design rules and carry insurance.
Renters pay for installation; the landlord may charge for electricity, upgrades and a reasonable access fee.

rtc.renters: Yes, landlord must approve a written request (phased in by landlord size; all landlords since October 2024)
points: The association cannot ban a charger or add rules that raise its cost or cut its performance.
You get approval, use a licensed contractor, provide insurance and pay for electricity and upkeep.
Renters pay for installation and removal; a charger left behind becomes part of the property.
A condo association cannot prohibit a charger in your own parking space, only add reasonable rules.
You use a licensed contractor and pay for installation, operation and repairs.
A condo association cannot prohibit a charger in your own parking space.
It can ask for a licensed contractor, a certificate of insurance, and repayment of any insurance premium increase.
You may install a charger at your stall if it meets the rules and you register it with the association within 30 days.
The association can restrict placement but cannot prevent it or charge a fee for it. A common-area charger needs its consent.

rtc.renters: Yes, a tenant may install a Level 1 or Level 2 charger at their space
points: The association cannot prohibit a charger in your space or add rules that raise its cost or cut its performance.
You use a licensed contractor, provide a certificate of insurance within 14 days and every year after, and pay for electricity.
Renters: the landlord may charge for electricity, network fees, any wiring upgrades, and a deposit to restore the space.
An association cannot prohibit or unreasonably restrict a charger in your exclusive-use space.
Your application counts as approved if it isn’t denied in writing within 60 days.
You pay for installation, upkeep and electricity, on your own meter where feasible.
An association cannot prohibit a charger in your own parking space and must treat it like any other architectural change.
You use a licensed contractor and pay for installation, insurance, upkeep and removal.
An association cannot prohibit a charger in your designated space.
You can apply to put one in a common space with the written consent of the owners who use it.
You pay for installation and electricity, carry insurance, and must tell a buyer the charger is there.
An association cannot prohibit a charger in your own parking space or add rules that significantly raise its cost.
You use a licensed contractor, provide a certificate of insurance and pay for installation and upkeep.
Neither an HOA nor a condo association can prohibit a charger in your own parking space.
Condos can ask for a licensed contractor and a certificate of insurance; you pay for installation and upkeep.

rtc.renters: Yes, landlord must act on an application within 60 days
points: An HOA must approve a complete application within 60 days or give you written reasonable conditions.

Renters: a landlord can refuse only if the property has fewer parking spaces than units. A licensed electrician does the work, you pay, and you carry $100,000 of liability insurance if the charger isn’t certified.
You pay for installation, electricity and removal, and must tell a buyer about the charger.
An HOA cannot prohibit a charger in your own parking space, but can set rules on size, placement and insurance outside the house.
A condo can refuse if it is not technically feasible or safe.

rtc.hoa: HOAs, condos and unit-owner associations (2025 law)
points: An association cannot prohibit a charger in your personal parking space.
You hire an experienced electrical contractor, provide a certificate of insurance, register the charger and pay for electricity until it is removed.
